name: Water memory

card.summary: The proposal that water retains a structural imprint of substances once dissolved in it, put forward to explain homeopathic dilutions and sometimes invoked in water-based skincare and wellness claims.
card.note: Not accepted by the scientific community.

quick.overview:
Water memory is the hypothesis that water keeps a lasting imprint of substances dissolved in it, even after they are diluted away. It is mostly discussed as a proposed mechanism for homeopathic remedies, and some beauty and wellness products invoke structured or charged water for skin.

The idea arose from Jacques Benveniste's laboratory in the late 1980s. Replication attempts, including a Nature-supervised investigation in 1988, did not reproduce the effect, and the scientific community does not accept it.
quick.how: In practice it appears as homeopathic dilutions or marketing of structured water products.
quick.risks: The concept itself carries no direct risk; concerns relate to replacing evidence-based treatment with remedies.

lead: Water memory is the proposal that water retains a trace of substances dissolved in it after dilution; homeopaths have taken it seriously because it could explain how highly diluted remedies act.[1][2] Its relevance to appearance is through homeopathic and water-based skincare or wellness products that cite it.

In 1988 Jacques Benveniste's group at INSERM published a Nature paper reporting that basophils responded to extremely diluted antibody solutions. Editor John Maddox asked readers to suspend judgement, then led a team including James Randi that observed re-runs; blinded runs showed no effect.[1] Later replication attempts, including a US Defense Department-funded one, failed to reproduce it.[1] Benveniste disputed the fairness of the tests.[1]

Supporters continue to propose mechanisms: a 2006 review in the Journal of the Royal Society for the Promotion of Health argued that dynamic ordering of hydrogen bonds could be a basis, and a 2007 paper reviewed the history from Benveniste's perspective.[3][4] Wikipedia describes water memory as pseudoscientific and not accepted by the scientific community.[1]

chain: Water said to hold an imprint
Remedies or water products cite this
angle.text: The idea is cited by makers of homeopathic and structured-water products who claim benefits for skin and health.

paras: The 1988 Nature paper reported high-dilution effects only when solutions were shaken; Maddox's team concluded that blinded trials showed no effect.[1]

Proponents including Benveniste continued to report effects, later claiming transmission by electromagnetic means.[4] Peter Fisher, editor of Homeopathy, acknowledged the method was not reproducible.[1]
No studies found. Laboratory experiments on high dilutions are summarised above; Louis Rey (2003) and Luc Montagnier (2009) claims have not been generally accepted.[1]

timeline.event: Benveniste's Nature paper; Maddox-led investigation follows.[1]
Special issue of Homeopathy examines mechanisms.[1][4]
